title: Crawler Log Folder
description: Brute force to optimized: a stack of folder names versus a single integer depth counter, since only the depth is ever queried.

blocks.text: The Leetcode file system keeps a log of file operations, given as a list of strings logs, where each entry is one of: "../" (move to the parent folder, if not already at the main folder), "./" (stay in the same folder), or "x/" (move to a child folder named x). Return the MINIMUM number of "../" operations needed to go back to the main folder after processing every log entry.

blocks.caption: Only the current nesting DEPTH matters; a stack of actual folder names is unnecessary since names are never queried

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An array of strings, each one of \"../\", \"./\", or \"x/\" (a named child folder)"],["Output","The minimum number of \"../\" moves needed to return to the main folder"],["Goal","Track the folder nesting depth, since that alone determines the answer"],["Constraints","1 <= logs.length <= 10^3; logs[i] is one of \"../\", \"./\", or a lowercase folder name followed by \"/\""]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Go to parent folder\" and \"enter a child folder\" mirror push/pop","A stack directly models a file system's folder navigation"],["The answer only asks HOW MANY moves to reach the root, never any actual folder NAME","The stack's actual contents (names) never matter, only its final SIZE (depth), so a simple counter replaces it entirely"]]}

blocks.text: Navigating folders behaves exactly like a stack: entering a child folder pushes it, going to the parent pops the most recent one (never going below the root), and staying in place does nothing; the final answer is simply how deep the current folder is nested, which is exactly how many "../" moves are needed to reach the root.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting How Many Doors Away You Are From the Building's Entrance
blocks.text: Imagine walking through a building by opening doors: entering a room goes one door deeper, going back through the door you just came from returns one level up (but you cannot go further back than the building's entrance), and standing still does nothing. The number of doors you would need to walk back through to reach the entrance is exactly how deep you currently are, which is all this problem is really asking for.

blocks.caption: Only three possible moves exist: enter a child folder (+1 depth), return to the parent (-1 depth, floored at 0), or stay (+0)

blocks.text: Before literally simulating a stack of folder names (which the problem does not actually require, since names are never queried), notice that only the CURRENT DEPTH matters, letting a simple integer counter replace the entire stack.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A stack of actual folder names would correctly simulate the file system, but the problem only ever asks for a COUNT of moves back to the root, never any folder's actual name.

Observation 2: Since the answer only depends on the current DEPTH (how many folders deep the current position is), the entire stack can be replaced by a single integer counter representing exactly that depth.

Observation 3: Entering a named child folder increases the depth by 1 (equivalent to pushing); "../" decreases the depth by 1 (equivalent to popping), but must never go below 0 (never popping past the root); "./" leaves the depth unchanged.

Observation 4: The final depth, after processing every log entry, is exactly the answer, since it represents exactly how many "../" moves would be needed to walk back to the root from the current position.
This is a simplification of the "stack models folder navigation" pattern: since only the DEPTH (stack size) is ever needed, a plain integer counter replaces the stack entirely.
Actually simulate the file system using a stack of folder names: push on entering a child folder, pop on "../" (if not empty), do nothing on "./". The answer is the final stack's size.

items: Maintain a stack of folder names.
For each log: push the folder name if entering a child, pop if going to the parent (and the stack is non-empty), or do nothing if staying in place.
The final stack's size is the answer.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A stack directly and faithfully simulates the actual file system navigation described in the problem.
The stack's final SIZE is exactly what the problem asks for, though the stack ALSO stores unnecessary information (the actual folder names).

blocks.text: Correctly simulates the folder navigation and produces the right answer, since a stack faithfully mirrors how folder depth changes with each operation.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass through the logs.
Space: O(n), for the stack of folder names in the worst case.

Limitation: the stack stores folder NAMES that are never actually needed by the problem; since only the current DEPTH (the stack's size) is ever queried, a single integer counter achieves the identical result with O(1) extra space.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force stores full folder names in a stack, but the problem only ever asks for a depth COUNT. Instead, track a single integer depth: increment it for a child folder, decrement it (floored at 0) for "../", and leave it unchanged for "./". The final depth value directly answers the question.
Initialize depth = 0. For each log: if "../", set depth to max(0, depth - 1); if "./", do nothing; otherwise (a named child folder), increment depth. Return the final depth.
Track a single integer depth counter directly, since the actual folder names are never needed.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The final depth is 3, matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single linear pass.
Space: O(1) extra, just a single integer counter.

Since the answer only ever asks "how many parent-folder moves are needed to reach the root," this is EXACTLY the current depth (nesting level), which is precisely what a stack's SIZE would be, without needing to know anything about which specific folder names are involved. Tracking just the depth as an integer discards only the unused information (the names), keeping everything that actually matters.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["\"x/\" (a named child folder)","depth increases by 1"],["\"../\" while depth > 0","depth decreases by 1"],["\"../\" while depth == 0 (already at the root)","depth stays at 0 (floored, cannot go negative)"],["\"./\"","depth stays unchanged"]]}

items: The max(0, depth - 1) (or equivalent floor logic) correctly prevents attempting to move above the root folder, exactly matching the real file system's behavior of ignoring an invalid "../" at the root.
No actual folder names are ever stored, since the problem never asks about them, only about the final depth.
The final depth value directly IS the answer, since returning to the root requires exactly that many "../" operations.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (stack of folder names)","O(n)","O(n)","Faithfully simulates the file system, but stores unnecessary folder names"],["Optimized (single integer depth counter)","O(n)","O(1)","Discards the unused folder names, keeping only the depth that actually matters"]]}

blocks.text: When a stack-based simulation is only ever QUERIED for its SIZE (never its actual contents), the stack can often be replaced entirely by a single counter, reducing space usage from O(n) to O(1) without losing any needed information.

items: Forgetting to floor the depth at 0 for "../" when already at the root, which would incorrectly allow a negative depth.
Overcomplicating the solution with an actual stack of folder names when only the depth was ever needed.
Mishandling the string comparisons (e.g., comparing against "..") instead of the full "../" and "./" tokens as given in the problem.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["All logs are \"../\"  starting from the root","The depth stays at 0 throughout, since it is floored and never goes negative"],["All logs are child-folder entries","The depth simply increases by 1 for each one"],["A mix that returns exactly to the root at the end","The final depth is 0, meaning 0 further moves are needed"]]}

items: Explicitly stating "the stack's contents are never queried, only its size, so a counter suffices" demonstrates the key space-optimization insight clearly and directly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Simulate folder/directory navigation, and only the DEPTH (not actual folder names) matters" points toward replacing a stack entirely with a simple counter.

items: When would the actual folder NAMES matter, requiring a real stack instead of just a counter? If the problem asked to return the FULL current path (not just its depth), the actual names would need to be tracked in a genuine stack.
How would you handle malformed logs (e.g., unexpected formats)? The problem's constraints guarantee well-formed logs, but a real-world implementation would need explicit validation.

How does this compare to Simplify Path elsewhere in this category? Simplify Path DOES need the actual folder names (since it must return the simplified path string), so it genuinely requires a stack, unlike this counter-only simplification.
A simplified variant of the stack-based folder-navigation pattern used more fully in Simplify Path elsewhere in this category, here reduced to just a counter since only the depth is ever queried.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (single integer depth counter): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Stack-simulation-as-a-counter (depth tracking)

Core Idea: Since only the current folder depth is ever queried (never actual folder names), a single integer counter replaces an entire stack, incrementing on child-folder entry and decrementing (floored at 0) on "../"
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: When a stack-based simulation is only ever asked for its SIZE, not its contents, it can be replaced entirely by a counter
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: "x/"=depth++, "../"=depth=max(0,depth-1), "./"=no change; final depth is the answer
